summary: An excerpt from a fiction book (Book 1, part 99) in which a character, recounting the 1960s, describes how UC Berkeley's campus information-table recruiting for civil rights and the Freedom Riders led to the Free Speech Movement and the rise of radical student groups. The narrator then explains the Yippies, a playful political group known for pranks such as trying to levitate the Pentagon and running a pig called Pigasus at the 1968 Democratic National Convention in Chicago. The passage ends with the Yippies' slogan 'Never trust anyone over 30.'
one_line: A fiction excerpt recounting Berkeley's Free Speech Movement and the prankster Yippies' 1960s protests, including the 1968 Chicago convention.
key_facts: Freedom Riders were recruited from information tables on campus at Bancroft and Telegraph Avenue.
The university president banned political organizing on campus, but civil rights students would not stop.
Police tried to arrest a student handing out literature from an information table and put him in a van.
About 3,000 students surrounded the van and refused to let it budge, standing on top of it to give speeches about the First Amendment and Free Speech.
The incident galvanized the Free Speech Movement, which the speaker describes as the start of the hippies and the origin of more radical student movements.
Radical groups that grew from this included the Black Panthers, the Pink Panthers, radical women's groups, and 'lesbian separatists.'
The Yippies were described as very political hippies who were playful pranksters rather than serious politicians.
The Yippies threw money into the New York Stock Exchange.
The Yippies circled the Pentagon with hundreds of protestors and said a magic spell that was supposed to levitate it.
A Yippie clown called Wavy Gravy got hundreds of protestors to dress up as Santa Claus so cameras would show police arresting Santa on the news.
The Yippies' big moment was the Democratic National Convention in 1968, where they protested the Vietnam War.
Thousands of demonstrators poured into Chicago in 1968, slept in the parks, and picketed every day.
The Yippies ran a pig called Pigasus for the presidential nomination.
Chicago police beat up reporters, and the resulting coverage led the country to call the clashes a 'police riot.'
The Yippies' slogan was 'Never trust anyone over 30.'
